subject: Banking
title: How to Read Your Credit Report
description: A fast breakdown of How to Read Your Credit Report for builders.

hook.text: A credit report looks like admin clutter, but one bad line can raise rates or kill an application.

buildup.text: The report has four sections: personal info, account history, inquiries, and public records like bankruptcies or liens.

discovery.text: Account history shows each account's credit limit, balance, payment status, and whether it's current or delinquent.

twist.text: Negative items stay for 7 years. Bankruptcies stay for 10. But their impact on your score fades each year.

climax.text: Your credit report is public knowledge to lenders. Understanding what's in it is the first step to controlling it.

punchline.text: Seven years of history. Lenders see everything. You should see it first.

quiz.question: How long do negative items typically stay on a credit report?

details.summary: A credit report contains your personal information, credit account history, public records like bankruptcies, and a list of everyone who has checked your credit. Learning to read it lets you spot errors, fraud, and areas for improvement.
details.whyItMatters: Your credit report is the foundation of your financial life, yet most people have never read theirs. Errors are common and can cost you thousands in higher interest rates or even loan denials that you might not know to challenge.
takeaways: Reports contain account history, payment records, and inquiry lists
You are entitled to one free report from each bureau annually
Account statuses, balance histories, and inquiry types all matter

faq.question: Where can you get your credit report for free?
faq.answer: AnnualCreditReport.com is the only federally authorized source for free reports from all three bureaus. Since the pandemic, free weekly reports are available. Avoid sites that require credit card information to access your free report.

faq.question: What is the difference between a hard and soft inquiry?
faq.answer: Hard inquiries occur when you apply for credit and can lower your score by a few points. Soft inquiries happen when you check your own credit or when companies prescreen you for offers. Soft inquiries do not affect your score at all.
